subject: MRDS - Line transect with pointing dogs

messages.author: c91d7ab8b6e98e86
messages.subject: MRDS - Line transect with pointing dogs
parts:
I measure autumn densities of grouse prior to commencement of hunting. Th=
e=20
main goal of the censuses is to monitor whether hunting affects populatio=
n=20
development thus precise estimates of change in different areas are=20
needed. The design is with permanent lines visiting the same set of=20
transects each year to get an estimate of trend with high precision. I us=
e=20
pointing dogs to find grouse while walking the line transects. When the=20=

dog finds a grouse it freezes and it is possible for the dog handler to=20=

walk to the dog and then give commando to flush the birds. Test on radio-=

collared grouse shows no responsive movements. The lines are walked by at=
=20
least two persons; one handles the dog and one keep track of the line=20
transect. When the birds are flushed the perpendicular distances from the=
=20
birds original place to the line transect are measured. The person=20
keeping track of the line has often more than two dogs in leach so the=20=

dogs that are on search can be altered. This means that on the line there=
=20
are always at least one man and two or more dogs and the dog handler.=20
Crisscrossing ahead of this equipage is one dog at the time on search for=
=20
grouse. It is not unusual that the equipage on the line flushes grouse=20=

independent of the dog on search. The same situation with man flushing=20=

grouse can happened when the dog handler leaves the line transect and=20
approaches the dog on stand (although this is not as common as flushing i=
s=20
directly on the line). Dog-flushing and man-flushing=92s are distinguishe=
d=20
and registered with perpendicular distance on the field protocol.=20
Is it possible to treat the equipage on the line and the dog on search as=
=20
two teams of observers? The equipage on the line searches on and close to=
=20
the line and the second team (dog) searches ahead of the equipage. The=20=

equipage on the line acts independently of the dog and will always see th=
e=20
same animal as the dog (duplicate sightings). Duplicates only occur if th=
e=20
dog sees the bird first. The birds flushed by the equipage on the line ar=
e=20
missed observations for the dog. P(0) for the equipage on the line will b=
e=20
1 and the pooled p(0) is 1. Can I treat this as a Buckland-Turnock mode,=20=

where the secondary observer is aware of the sightings of the primary=20
observer in a trial configuration because of only one-way independence?=20=
=20
My intention is to estimate p(0) for the dog and use this in a second=20
analysis where I delete all observations not made by the dog and then=20
adjust for g(0)<1 in a traditional distance sampling analysis. Am I=20
thinking right here?

--

messages.author: 5140016d70f6ba82
messages.subject: Re: MRDS - Line transect with pointing dogs
parts:
Maria-

Your thinking is close but not quite correct. What you have is a=20
removal design. The dog ahead sees birds and the equipage behind also=20
sees them so they are effectively "removed" as a trial for the=20
equipage. The only ones that are missed are "01" and by definition you=20
cannot have any "10" where the dog "sees" a bird and the equipage does=20
not. I understand that you want to flip this around and use the=20
"11"/("11" + "01") as an estimate of p(0) for the dog. This will give a=20
valid estimate as long as the equipage does not miss any birds. If the=20
equipage does miss birds then your estimate of p(0) for the dogs will be=20
too high and your estimate of abundance from the dogs will be too low. =20
You can avoid that bias by fitting a removal model to estimate p(0) but=20
that necessarily assumes that p(0) is the same for the equipage and the=20
birds which it doesn't sound like it is. I'm not quite sure why you=20
propose to do this unless you are going to run transects without the=20
equipage. If so then you can use the naive estimator above but beware=20
that it will be biased if p(0)<1 for the equipage.

regards --jeff
